Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States
Title: History of education in the United States
Chunks: 36,37,38,39,40,62,63,64,65,66
### Colleges in 19th century
#### Schools for Black students
[edit]
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Freedmen's_school,_Edisto_Island,_S.C.)_-_Samuel_A._Cooley,_photographer,_Savannah,_Ga.,_Hilton_Head,_S.C.,_Beaufort,_S.C_LCCN2010647918_(cropped).jpg)
The Freedmen's School of Edisto Island, South Carolina photographed c.1865
In the early days of the Reconstruction era, the [Freedmen's Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedmen's_Bureau "Freedmen's Bureau") opened 1000 schools across the South for black children. This was essentially building on schools that had been established in numerous large contraband camps. Freedmen were eager for schooling for both adults and children, and the enrollments were high and enthusiastic. Overall, the Bureau spent $5 million to set up schools for blacks. By the end of 1865, more than 90,000 freedmen were enrolled as students in these schools. The school curriculum resembled that of schools in the North.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-127)

### Colleges in 19th century
#### Schools for Black students
Many Bureau teachers were well-educated Yankee women motivated by religion and abolitionism. W.E.B. DuBois wrote of the zealous spirit and success of what he referred to as "the crusade of the New England schoolma'am."[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-128) Half the teachers were southern whites; one-third were blacks, and one-sixth were northern whites.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-129) Most were women but among African Americans, male teachers slightly outnumbered female teachers. In the South, people were attracted to teaching because of the good salaries, at a time when the societies were disrupted and the economy was poor. Northern teachers were typically funded by northern organizations and were motivated by humanitarian goals to help the freedmen. As a group, only the black cohort showed a commitment to racial equality; they were also the ones most likely to continue as teachers.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-130)
When the Republicans came to power in the Southern states after 1867, they created the first system of taxpayer-funded public schools. Southern Blacks wanted public schools for their children but they did not demand racially integrated schools. Almost all the new public schools were segregated, apart from a few in New Orleans. After the Republicans lost power in the mid-1870s, conservative whites retained the public school systems but sharply cut their funding. [[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-131)
Howard University was founded in 1867, making it one of a number of historically black colleges and universities established after the American Civil War

### Colleges in 19th century
#### Schools for Black students
Almost all private academies and colleges in the South were strictly segregated by race.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-132) The American Missionary Association supported the development and establishment of several historically black colleges, such as Fisk University and Shaw University. In this period, a handful of northern colleges accepted black students. The Oneida Institute of Science and Industry (founded 1827) was the first institution of higher education to routinely admit African-American men and provide mixed-race college-level education.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-133) Oberlin College (founded 1833) was the first mainly white, degree-granting college to admit African-American students.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-134) However, before the Civil War it is likely that only 3–5% of Oberlin students were African-American.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-135) By 1900, 400 African-Americans had earned B.A. degrees from Harvard, Yale, Oberlin, and 70 other "leading colleges."[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-136) Northern denominations and their missionary associations especially established private schools across the South to provide secondary education. They provided a small amount of collegiate work. Tuition was minimal, so churches supported the colleges financially, and also subsidized the pay of some teachers. In 1900, churches—mostly based in the North—operated 247 schools for blacks across the South, with a budget of about $1 million.

### Colleges in 19th century
#### Schools for Black students
They employed 1600 teachers and taught 46,000 students.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-137)[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-138) Prominent schools included Howard University, a federal institution based in Washington; Fisk University in Nashville, Atlanta University, Hampton Institute in Virginia, and many others. Most new colleges in the 19th century were founded in northern states.
In 1890, Congress expanded the land-grant program to include federal support for state-sponsored colleges across the South. It required states to identify colleges for black students as well as white ones in order to get land grant support. This second Morrill Land-Grant Act thus simultaneously provided increased higher educational opportunities for African Americans but encouraged segregation.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-139)

### Colleges in 19th century
#### Schools for Black students
Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute was of national importance because it set the standards for what was called industrial education.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnderson198833%E2%80%9378-140)Booker T. Washington, one of its graduates, founded the influential Tuskegee Normal School for Colored Teachers in 1881. Washington championed industrial education for African Americans on the basis of its practicality, whereas W.E.B. DuBois emphasized the importance of offering African Americans the opportunity to prove themselves equal to whites by succeeding in traditional, classically-oriented B.A. degree programs.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-141) In 1900 relatively few black students were enrolled in college-level work because their schools were understaffed and underfunded and the students needed remedial study. The alumni of Keithley became high school teachers.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-142) However, some HBCUs—such as Howard University, Fisk University, and Atlanta University—had standard B.A. programs with classical curricula.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-143)
While the colleges and academies were generally coeducational, until the late 20th century, historians had taken little notice of the role of women as students and teachers.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-144)

### Consolidation: the passing of the one room schoolhouse
#### Growth of human capital
American post-elementary schooling was designed to be consistent with national needs. It stressed general and widely applicable skills not tied to particular occupations or geographic areas, in order that students would have flexible employment options. As the economy was dynamic, the emphasis was on portable skills that could be used in a variety of occupations, industries, and regions.[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-205)
Public schools were funded and supervised by independent districts that depended on taxpayer support. In dramatic contrast to the centralized systems in Europe, where national agencies made the major decisions, the American districts designed their own rules and curricula.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-206)

### Consolidation: the passing of the one room schoolhouse
#### Teachers and administrators
[edit]
Early public school superintendents emphasized discipline and rote learning, and school principals made sure the mandate was imposed on teachers. Disruptive students were expelled.[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-207)
Support for the high school movement occurred at the grass-roots level of local cities and school systems. After 1916, the federal government began to provide for vocational education funding as part of support for raising readiness to work in industrial and artisan jobs. In these years, states and religious bodies generally funded teacher training colleges, often called "normal schools". Gradually they developed full four-year curriculums and developed as state colleges after 1945.
Teachers organized themselves during the 1920s and 1930s. In 1917, the National Education Association (NEA) was reorganized to better mobilize and represent teachers and educational staff. The rate of increase in membership was constant under the chairmanship of James Crabtree—from 8,466 members in 1917 to 220,149 in 1931. The rival American Federation of Teachers (AFT) was based in large cities and formed alliances with the local labor unions. The NEA identified as an upper-middle-class professional organization, while the AFT identified with the working class and the union movement.[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-208)[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-209)

### Consolidation: the passing of the one room schoolhouse
#### Teachers and administrators
When liberals regained control of Congress in 1964, they passed numerous Great Society programs supported by President Lyndon B. Johnson to expand federal support for education. The Higher Education Act of 1965 set up federal scholarships and low-interest loans for college students, and subsidized better academic libraries, ten to twenty new graduate centers, several new technical institutes, classrooms for several hundred thousand students, and twenty-five to thirty new community colleges a year. A separate education bill enacted that same year provided similar assistance to dental and medical schools. On an even larger scale, the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965 began pumping federal money into local school districts.[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-210)

### Segregation and integration
[edit]
Segregation laws in the United States prior to _Brown v. Board of Education_
For much of its history, education in the United States was segregated (or even only available) based upon race. Early integrated schools such as the Noyes Academy, founded in 1835, in Canaan, New Hampshire, often were met with fierce local opposition. For the most part, African Americans received very little to no formal education before the Civil War. Some free blacks in the North managed to become literate. In cities, such a Philadelphia and New York City, they founded literary societies for self-education, as well as some academies for their children. The most prominent of the latter was Philadelphia's Institute for Colored Youth, the nation's first coeducational high school for African Americans.[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-211) A few institutions of higher education also were available to African Americans in the North. The Oneida Institute of Science and Industry was the first such entity to recruit and commonly admit African American men. New York Central College also was mixed race, and Oberlin College was the first B.A. degree-granting, white college to accept African Americans. In 1840, Oberlin bestowed the first known B.A. degree on an African American--George B. Vashon, who later was a founding member of the Howard University faculty.[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-212)

### Segregation and integration
In the South where slavery was legal, many states had laws prohibiting teaching enslaved African Americans to read or write.[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-213) A few taught themselves, sometimes in secret schools,[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-214) others learned from white playmates or more generous masters, but most were not able to learn to read and write. Schools for free people of color were privately run and supported, as were most of the limited schools for white children. Poor white children did not attend school. The wealthier planters hired tutors for their children and sent them to private academies and colleges at the appropriate age.
During Reconstruction a coalition of freedmen and white Republicans in Southern state legislatures passed laws establishing public education. The [Freedmen's Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedmen's_Bureau "Freedmen's Bureau") was created as an agency of the military governments that managed Reconstruction. It set up schools in many areas and tried to help educate and protect freedmen during the transition after the war. With the notable exception of the desegregated public schools in New Orleans, the schools were segregated by race. By 1900 more than 30,000 black teachers had been trained and put to work in the South, and the literacy rate had climbed to more than 50%, a major achievement in little more than a generation.[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnderson1988244%E2%80%93245-215)
Many colleges were set up for blacks; some were state schools like Booker T. Washington's Tuskegee Institute in Alabama, others were private ones subsidized by Northern missionary societies.

Title: Research Guides: African American Women: Home

Civil rights and women's rights activist Dorothy Irene Height graduated from New York University (BA and MA in educational psychology, 1932, 1933). She began her career as a case worker with the New York City Welfare Department and at the age of 25 joined the National Council of Negro Women, an organization that she led for 40 years (1957-1997). Under its auspices she founded Wednesdays in Mississippi, during which Northern women of different races and faiths would travel to Mississippi to foster understanding across regional, racial, and class lines. Height also was a member of the national staff of the Young Women's Christian Association, and an active member of Delta Sigma Theta Sorority, where she served as national president (1947-1956). She was a founding member of the Council for United Civil Rights Leadership, and a regular adviser to American leaders, including Eleanor Roosevelt, Dwight D. Eisenhower, and Lyndon B. Johnson. Height was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1994 and the Congressional Gold Medal in 2004. The papers of Dorothy I. Height include correspondence, organizational records, photographs, audiovisual materials, memorabilia and other materials documenting Height's 50-year term as President of the National Council of Negro Women and work on behalf of other organizations.
*   Gattie Holmes

Gattie Holmes was a single professional African American woman whose music career teaching piano spanned from the 1940s through the 1990s. She was the daughter of a Canadian Native American mother and an African American father. As a child Holmes lived in New Haven, Connecticut, where her father owned a candy store. Holmes was a very musical child and her parents enrolled her in the Royal College of Music in London when she was a teenager. Either in Europe or later in the United States, she studied with the Austrian American classical pianist Arthur Schnabel and with the pianist Lee Pattison, who built the music program at Scripps College in Claremont, California. Pattison recruited Holmes and she moved out to Claremont, California where she built a house and business as a music instructor. At some point, possibly from when Holmes attended the Royal College of Music, she began passing for white. She spent her entire professional career in Claremont, California, and participated in the Los Angeles music scene, without others being aware of her ethnic heritage. The collection includes correspondence; notebooks; sheet music; newspaper articles; music notebooks; and more. The materials document Holmes' personal life, music career, and other creative projects and interests.
*   [Lena Horne [in Gail Lumet Buckley Papers]](http://id.lib.harvard.edu/alma/99153684315803941/catalog)
The portion of the collection relating to Lena Horne includes Horne's awards and honorary degrees; fliers, programs and posters from her performances; clippings; scrapbooks; and Horne's own reflections about her life and career. Of particular interest is material related to her musical tour, "Lena Horne: The Lady and Her Music, "which toured in the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom from 1981 until 1984. Notebooks from the tour include photographs, drawings, fabric swatches and detailed accounts of each outfit worn on stage; as well as guest lists, programs, and reviews for the shows are also included. Also of interest are the Horne family papers, Horne's correspondence, and personal papers.
*   Pat Matthews Howard (b. 1918) This link opens in a new window

Pat Matthews Howard worked as a school teacher, secretary, and for the Yellow Springs News in Ohio. She was active in the civil rights movement and was interested in the history of Black people in Yellow Springs, helping a class write a book on local Black history and interviewing older members of the Black community. Howard’s collection mainly consists of interview transcripts.
*   Mary Gibson Hundley (1897-1986) This link opens in a new window
An educator and civil rights activist, Hundley attended Radcliffe College from 1914-1918. In 1927, she pursued graduate studies at Middlebury College in Vermont and a year later at the Sorbonne in France. After graduation she taught at the Dunbar School, Eastern High School, and at Howard University, all in Washington, D.C.
*   Ellen Jackson (1935-2005) This link opens in a new window
Ellen Swepson Jackson was the founder and executive director of Operation Exodus, a program organized to bus inner-city students from Boston to suburban schools. She later co-authored _Family Experiences in Operation Exodus, Inc._ (1967), and served as dean and director of affirmative action at Northeastern University from 1978 to 1997.
*   Anna Louise James (1886-1977) This link opens in a new window
The first African American woman to become a licensed pharmacist in Connecticut, Anna Louise James was born in Hartford. She attended local schools and graduated from Arsenal Elementary School (1902) and Saybrook High School (1905). She graduated from the Brooklyn College of Pharmacy in 1908 and returned to Hartford, where she operated her own drug store from 1909 until 1911. She later moved to Old Saybrook, where she continued to operate a pharmacy and became active in Republican Party politics. James was one of the first women in Old Saybrook to register to vote after the passage of the 19th Amendment in 1920.
*   Mildred Jefferson (1926-2010) This link opens in a new window

Mildred Jefferson was the first Black woman to graduate from Harvard Medical School (1951) and the first woman employed as a surgeon at Boston University Medical Center. Jefferson became involved in the pro-life movement in 1970. She was a founding member of the Value of Life Committee (VOLCOM) in Massachusetts and subsequently helped formed Massachusetts Citizens for Life (MCFL), which was incorporated in 1973. MCFL's efforts led to the founding of the National Right to Life Committee (NRTLC), an umbrella organization comprising 50 state-run organizations and more than 3000 local chapters. She advised and influenced local, state, and national candidates on pro-life issues and actively campaigned on their behalf. Jefferson received numerous awards and citations for her contributions to the pro-life movement.
*   Darlene Jeter This link opens in a new window
Darlene Jeter was the president of Jet-A-Way, a recycling and waste disposal company based in Boston. Founded in 1969 by her and her husband Eddie, by 1996 the company was one of the largest minority-owned businesses in the city. Trained as a practical nurse, Darlene Jeter began her work for the company as a bookkeeper and office manager. After her husband's death in 1991, she became president and expanded the company's range of services and clientele. The collection includes mostly printed material about Jet-A-Way and Darlene and Eddie Jeter; also some correspondence and audiovisual material.
*   Kathryn M. Johnson (b. 1878) This link opens in a new window

Educator Kathryn Magnolia Johnson attended Wilberforce University, where she earned a teaching certificate and BA. She taught in Ohio, North Carolina, and Kansas City, Kan., and later served as Dean of Women at Shorter College in Little Rock, Ark. (1906). In Kansas City, she also helped establish a Young Women's Christian Association for African Americans. In 1913 she conducted field work for the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, selling Crisis magazine and organizing branches in Kansas City, Topeka, and Oklahoma. During World War I, Johnson went to France with the American Expeditionary Forces and described the experience in _Two Colored Women with the American Expeditionary Forces_ (1920), which she co-authored with Addie D. Hunton. After the war, Johnson traveled widely, lecturing on African American history.
*   June Jordan (1936-2002) This link opens in a new window
An award-winning author, poet, and social and political activist, June Jordan was born in Harlem, New York and attended public schools in Brooklyn. She graduated from Northfield School for Girls in 1953, attended Barnard College (1953-1955), and enrolled in the University of Chicago for a year. She returned to New York and briefly resumed studies at Barnard and Hunter College (1962). Shortly after she withdrew from college, Jordan became involved in urban development and conducted research for Mobilization for Youth, Inc., on the Lower East Side of Manhattan and collaborated with R. Buckminster Fuller on an architectural redesign of Harlem. She also received an award for creative writing from the Rockefeller Foundation (1969) along with the Prix de Rome in Environmental Design (1970). A prolific writer, Jordan produced fiction and nonfiction while successfully pursuing a teaching career.
*   Maida Springer Kemp (1910-2005) This link opens in a new window

*   Florence Cawthorne Ladd (b. 1932)
Florence Cawthorne Ladd is a graduate of Howard University (B.S. 1953) and the University of Rochester (Ph.D. 1958), and has taught at. Simmons College, Robert College and the American College for Girls in Istanbul, and Harvard University's Graduate School of Education and Graduate School of Design. Shifting her focus to administration, Ladd was assistant, then associate dean at the MIT School of Architecture and Planning (1977-1979), dean of students at Wellesley College (1979-1984), director of education and outreach and later associate executive director at Oxfam America (1985-1989), and director of the Bunting Institute at Radcliffe College (1989-1997). Her first novel, _Sarah's Psalm_, was published in 1996 and received the Literary Award for Best Fiction from the Black Caucus of the American Library Association. Her second novel, _The Spirit of Josephine_, was published in 2014. She is also the co-author of the non-fiction work, _Is That Your Child? Mothers Talk about Rearing Biracial Children_ (2008). This collection contain drafts and reviews of Sarah's Psalm and The Spirit of Josephine; personal and literary correspondence; office files related to Ladd's tenure at Radcliffe College's Bunting Institute and Harvard's Graduate School of Design; photographs; and audio recordings of interviews with Ladd.
*   Links, Inc. Boston Chapter
Founded in 1950, the Links, Inc. Boston Chapter is a public service, non-partisan, volunteer organization of African American women. The membership seeks to enrich, sustain, and ensure the culture and economic survival of African Americans and other persons of African descent. Past fund-raising events include Ebony Fashion Fair, Carnaval, and Day at the Races. All Links chapters are mandated to developing programming related to four national program areas of: Services to Youth, National Trends and Services, The Arts, and International Trends and Services in order to support and strengthen African American communities and enhance the nation through education, civic, and cultural activities. The collection consists of photographs, financial material, and committee files.

*   Cora V. Reid MacKerrow (1890-1984) This link opens in a new window
Owner and operator of the Modern Funeral Home, MacKerrow was one of fifteen children born near Churchland, Virginia. After her mother died MacKerrow was sent to St. Paul's, an Episcopal boarding school in Lawrenceville, Va. She later moved to Boston and worked as a chiropodist and beautician. In 1926, she and her brother, Millard Fillmore Reid, opened the Modern Funeral Home on Dartmouth Street. After his death, she ran the business alone for thirty years, finally closing it in 1971. She also served as treasurer and vice-president of the Women's Service Club and as president of Harriet Tubman House.
*   Lucy Miller Mitchell (1899-2002) This link opens in a new window
A specialist in early childhood education, Lucy Miller Mitchell received her formative education at Daytona Normal and Industrial Institute. She graduated from Talladega College in 1922 and became active in the field of childhood education. After taking courses at the Nursery Training School with Abigail A. Eliot, she received certification in 1934 and was awarded a master's degree in early childhood education from Boston University in 1935. Mitchell served as director of the nursery school at Robert Gould Shaw House from 1932 to 1953 and developed practices that were adapted by other schools and by students new to the field. Additional information is included in the Black Women Oral History Project.
*   Irene Monroe (b. 1955)
An activist, theologian, journalist and motivational speaker, Reverend Monroe has written and lectured extensively on a broad range of social issues and on the history of African American, lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender communities in Boston and across the nation. She has taught classes on women’s healing and served on various boards, including the Cambridge Family YMCA and the National Black Justice Coalition. Her writings, which include columns, news features, and book reviews, have been published in _Chicken Bones: A Journal_, _In Newsweekly_, the _Boston Globe_, _The Other Side_, and _The Witness_. In addition to her papers, researchers can view her web site at www.irenemonroe.com, which is being archived by Harvard University.

*   Pauli Murray (1910-1985) This link opens in a new window
A lawyer, educator, political activist, and writer, Pauli Murray was the first woman to become an ordained Episcopal minister. She was born in Baltimore, Md., and grew up in North Carolina, where she was raised by her maternal aunt. Murray attended Hunter College in New York City and graduated in 1933. She held a variety of jobs with organizations such as the Works Progress Administration and the Workers' Defense League. She attended Howard University Law School (1941-1944) and completed graduate studies at the University of California, Berkeley. During the 1940s she operated a law office in New York City and was later hired as an associate attorney for the law offices of Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton, and Garrison (1956). During the 1960s Murray was a university professor and served on the President's Commission on the Status of Women.
*   National Association of Negro Business and Professional Women's Clubs
The National Association of Negro Business and Professional Women's Clubs was conceived in 1934 by Emma Odessa Young, a New York realtor and member of the New York Club of Business and Professional Women. In 1936, during its first convention, the organization elected Ollie Chinn Porter as its first president. The goal of the organization was to promote and protect the interests of Black professional women, encourage support and fellowship among members, direct interests toward united action for improved social and civic conditions, encourage the formation of subsidiary clubs throughout the United States, and create opportunities for Black women in business and the professions. Today, the organization continues to provide support to Black business women and the African American community at large.
*   National Institute for Women of Color

The National Institute for Women of Color (NIWC), founded in 1981 in the District of Columbia, was an independent non-profit organization created to promote the strengths of diversity along with educational and economic equity for women of color. Funded mainly through grants, NIWC was managed by its Board of Directors, with the help of state coordinators, a national advisory committee, and volunteers. NIWC was an advocacy group which acted as a networking center for women of color and focused on mutual concerns of education, housing, healthcare, and pay equity. NIWC's main objectives were to develop leadership skills in women, to recognize women of color leaders, to educate society about the status and basic needs of women of color, to provide a support network, and to advocate for changes in public policy. Civil rights and women's rights activist Dorothy Irene Height graduated from New York University (BA and MA in educational psychology, 1932, 1933). She began her career as a case worker with the New York City Welfare Department and at the age of 25 joined the National Council of Negro Women, an organization that she led for 40 years (1957-1997). Under its auspices she founded Wednesdays in Mississippi, during which Northern women of different races and faiths would travel to Mississippi to foster understanding across regional, racial, and class lines. Height also was a member of the national staff of the Young Women's Christian Association, and an active member of Delta Sigma Theta Sorority, where she served as national president (1947-1956). She was a founding member of the Council for United Civil Rights Leadership, and a regular adviser to American leaders, including Eleanor Roosevelt, Dwight D. Eisenhower, and Lyndon B. Johnson. Height was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1994 and the Congressional Gold Medal in 2004. The papers of Dorothy I. Height include correspondence, organizational records, photographs, audiovisual materials, memorabilia and other materials documenting Height's 50-year term as President of the National Council of Negro Women and work on behalf of other organizations.

texts.8:
Gattie Holmes was a single professional African American woman whose music career teaching piano spanned from the 1940s through the 1990s. She was the daughter of a Canadian Native American mother and an African American father. As a child Holmes lived in New Haven, Connecticut, where her father owned a candy store. Holmes was a very musical child and her parents enrolled her in the Royal College of Music in London when she was a teenager. Either in Europe or later in the United States, she studied with the Austrian American classical pianist Arthur Schnabel and with the pianist Lee Pattison, who built the music program at Scripps College in Claremont, California. Pattison recruited Holmes and she moved out to Claremont, California where she built a house and business as a music instructor. At some point, possibly from when Holmes attended the Royal College of Music, she began passing for white. She spent her entire professional career in Claremont, California, and participated in the Los Angeles music scene, without others being aware of her ethnic heritage. The collection includes correspondence; notebooks; sheet music; newspaper articles; music notebooks; and more. The materials document Holmes' personal life, music career, and other creative projects and interests.

Florence Cawthorne Ladd is a graduate of Howard University (B.S. 1953) and the University of Rochester (Ph.D. 1958), and has taught at. Simmons College, Robert College and the American College for Girls in Istanbul, and Harvard University's Graduate School of Education and Graduate School of Design. Founded in 1950, the Links, Inc. Boston Chapter is a public service, non-partisan, volunteer organization of African American women. ### Colleges in 19th century
#### Schools for Black students
[edit]
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Freedmen's_school,_Edisto_Island,_S.C.)_-_Samuel_A._Cooley,_photographer,_Savannah,_Ga.,_Hilton_Head,_S.C.,_Beaufort,_S.C_LCCN2010647918_(cropped).jpg)
The Freedmen's School of Edisto Island, South Carolina photographed c.1865
In the early days of the Reconstruction era, the [Freedmen's Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedmen's_Bureau "Freedmen's Bureau") opened 1000 schools across the South for black children. This was essentially building on schools that had been established in numerous large contraband camps. Freedmen were eager for schooling for both adults and children, and the enrollments were high and enthusiastic. Overall, the Bureau spent $5 million to set up schools for blacks. By the end of 1865, more than 90,000 freedmen were enrolled as students in these schools. The school curriculum resembled that of schools in the North.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-127)
texts.37:
### Colleges in 19th century
#### Schools for Black students
Many Bureau teachers were well-educated Yankee women motivated by religion and abolitionism. W.E.B. DuBois wrote of the zealous spirit and success of what he referred to as "the crusade of the New England schoolma'am."[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-128) Half the teachers were southern whites; one-third were blacks, and one-sixth were northern whites.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-129) Most were women but among African Americans, male teachers slightly outnumbered female teachers. In the South, people were attracted to teaching because of the good salaries, at a time when the societies were disrupted and the economy was poor. Northern teachers were typically funded by northern organizations and were motivated by humanitarian goals to help the freedmen. As a group, only the black cohort showed a commitment to racial equality; they were also the ones most likely to continue as teachers.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-130)
When the Republicans came to power in the Southern states after 1867, they created the first system of taxpayer-funded public schools. Southern Blacks wanted public schools for their children but they did not demand racially integrated schools. Almost all the new public schools were segregated, apart from a few in New Orleans. After the Republicans lost power in the mid-1870s, conservative whites retained the public school systems but sharply cut their funding. [[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-131)
Howard University was founded in 1867, making it one of a number of historically black colleges and universities established after the American Civil War
texts.38:
### Colleges in 19th century
#### Schools for Black students
Almost all private academies and colleges in the South were strictly segregated by race.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-132) The American Missionary Association supported the development and establishment of several historically black colleges, such as Fisk University and Shaw University. In this period, a handful of northern colleges accepted black students. The Oneida Institute of Science and Industry (founded 1827) was the first institution of higher education to routinely admit African-American men and provide mixed-race college-level education.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-133) Oberlin College (founded 1833) was the first mainly white, degree-granting college to admit African-American students.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-134) However, before the Civil War it is likely that only 3–5% of Oberlin students were African-American.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-135) By 1900, 400 African-Americans had earned B.A. degrees from Harvard, Yale, Oberlin, and 70 other "leading colleges."[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-136) Northern denominations and their missionary associations especially established private schools across the South to provide secondary education. They provided a small amount of collegiate work. Tuition was minimal, so churches supported the colleges financially, and also subsidized the pay of some teachers. In 1900, churches—mostly based in the North—operated 247 schools for blacks across the South, with a budget of about $1 million.
texts.39:
### Colleges in 19th century
#### Schools for Black students
They employed 1600 teachers and taught 46,000 students.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-137)[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-138) Prominent schools included Howard University, a federal institution based in Washington; Fisk University in Nashville, Atlanta University, Hampton Institute in Virginia, and many others. Most new colleges in the 19th century were founded in northern states.
In 1890, Congress expanded the land-grant program to include federal support for state-sponsored colleges across the South. It required states to identify colleges for black students as well as white ones in order to get land grant support. This second Morrill Land-Grant Act thus simultaneously provided increased higher educational opportunities for African Americans but encouraged segregation.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-139)
texts.40:
### Colleges in 19th century
#### Schools for Black students
Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute was of national importance because it set the standards for what was called industrial education.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnderson198833%E2%80%9378-140)Booker T. Washington, one of its graduates, founded the influential Tuskegee Normal School for Colored Teachers in 1881. Washington championed industrial education for African Americans on the basis of its practicality, whereas W.E.B. DuBois emphasized the importance of offering African Americans the opportunity to prove themselves equal to whites by succeeding in traditional, classically-oriented B.A. degree programs.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-141) In 1900 relatively few black students were enrolled in college-level work because their schools were understaffed and underfunded and the students needed remedial study. The alumni of Keithley became high school teachers.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-142) However, some HBCUs—such as Howard University, Fisk University, and Atlanta University—had standard B.A. programs with classical curricula.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-143)
While the colleges and academies were generally coeducational, until the late 20th century, historians had taken little notice of the role of women as students and teachers.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-144)
texts.62:
### Consolidation: the passing of the one room schoolhouse
#### Growth of human capital
American post-elementary schooling was designed to be consistent with national needs. It stressed general and widely applicable skills not tied to particular occupations or geographic areas, in order that students would have flexible employment options. As the economy was dynamic, the emphasis was on portable skills that could be used in a variety of occupations, industries, and regions.[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-205)
Public schools were funded and supervised by independent districts that depended on taxpayer support. In dramatic contrast to the centralized systems in Europe, where national agencies made the major decisions, the American districts designed their own rules and curricula.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-206)
texts.63:
### Consolidation: the passing of the one room schoolhouse
#### Teachers and administrators
[edit]
Early public school superintendents emphasized discipline and rote learning, and school principals made sure the mandate was imposed on teachers. Disruptive students were expelled.[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-207)
Support for the high school movement occurred at the grass-roots level of local cities and school systems. After 1916, the federal government began to provide for vocational education funding as part of support for raising readiness to work in industrial and artisan jobs. In these years, states and religious bodies generally funded teacher training colleges, often called "normal schools". Gradually they developed full four-year curriculums and developed as state colleges after 1945.
Teachers organized themselves during the 1920s and 1930s. In 1917, the National Education Association (NEA) was reorganized to better mobilize and represent teachers and educational staff. The rate of increase in membership was constant under the chairmanship of James Crabtree—from 8,466 members in 1917 to 220,149 in 1931. The rival American Federation of Teachers (AFT) was based in large cities and formed alliances with the local labor unions. The NEA identified as an upper-middle-class professional organization, while the AFT identified with the working class and the union movement.[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-208)[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-209)
texts.64:
### Consolidation: the passing of the one room schoolhouse
#### Teachers and administrators
When liberals regained control of Congress in 1964, they passed numerous Great Society programs supported by President Lyndon B. Johnson to expand federal support for education. The Higher Education Act of 1965 set up federal scholarships and low-interest loans for college students, and subsidized better academic libraries, ten to twenty new graduate centers, several new technical institutes, classrooms for several hundred thousand students, and twenty-five to thirty new community colleges a year. A separate education bill enacted that same year provided similar assistance to dental and medical schools. On an even larger scale, the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965 began pumping federal money into local school districts.[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-210)
texts.65:
### Segregation and integration
[edit]
Segregation laws in the United States prior to _Brown v. Board of Education_
For much of its history, education in the United States was segregated (or even only available) based upon race. Early integrated schools such as the Noyes Academy, founded in 1835, in Canaan, New Hampshire, often were met with fierce local opposition. For the most part, African Americans received very little to no formal education before the Civil War. Some free blacks in the North managed to become literate. In cities, such a Philadelphia and New York City, they founded literary societies for self-education, as well as some academies for their children. The most prominent of the latter was Philadelphia's Institute for Colored Youth, the nation's first coeducational high school for African Americans.[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-211) A few institutions of higher education also were available to African Americans in the North. The Oneida Institute of Science and Industry was the first such entity to recruit and commonly admit African American men. New York Central College also was mixed race, and Oberlin College was the first B.A. degree-granting, white college to accept African Americans. In 1840, Oberlin bestowed the first known B.A. degree on an African American--George B. Vashon, who later was a founding member of the Howard University faculty.[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-212)
texts.66:
### Segregation and integration
In the South where slavery was legal, many states had laws prohibiting teaching enslaved African Americans to read or write.[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-213) A few taught themselves, sometimes in secret schools,[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-214) others learned from white playmates or more generous masters, but most were not able to learn to read and write. Schools for free people of color were privately run and supported, as were most of the limited schools for white children. Poor white children did not attend school. The wealthier planters hired tutors for their children and sent them to private academies and colleges at the appropriate age.
During Reconstruction a coalition of freedmen and white Republicans in Southern state legislatures passed laws establishing public education. The [Freedmen's Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedmen's_Bureau "Freedmen's Bureau") was created as an agency of the military governments that managed Reconstruction. It set up schools in many areas and tried to help educate and protect freedmen during the transition after the war. With the notable exception of the desegregated public schools in New Orleans, the schools were segregated by race. By 1900 more than 30,000 black teachers had been trained and put to work in the South, and the literacy rate had climbed to more than 50%, a major achievement in little more than a generation.[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnderson1988244%E2%80%93245-215)
Many colleges were set up for blacks; some were state schools like Booker T. Washington's Tuskegee Institute in Alabama, others were private ones subsidized by Northern missionary societies.

In the early days of the Reconstruction era, the [Freedmen's Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedmen's_Bureau "Freedmen's Bureau") opened 1000 schools across the South for black children. This was essentially building on schools that had been established in numerous large contraband camps. Freedmen were eager for schooling for both adults and children, and the enrollments were high and enthusiastic. Overall, the Bureau spent $5 million to set up schools for blacks. By the end of 1865, more than 90,000 freedmen were enrolled as students in these schools. The school curriculum resembled that of schools in the North.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-127)

### Colleges in 19th century
#### Schools for Black students
Many Bureau teachers were well-educated Yankee women motivated by religion and abolitionism. W.E.B. DuBois wrote of the zealous spirit and success of what he referred to as "the crusade of the New England schoolma'am."[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-128) Half the teachers were southern whites; one-third were blacks, and one-sixth were northern whites.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-129) Most were women but among African Americans, male teachers slightly outnumbered female teachers. In the South, people were attracted to teaching because of the good salaries, at a time when the societies were disrupted and the economy was poor. Northern teachers were typically funded by northern organizations and were motivated by humanitarian goals to help the freedmen. As a group, only the black cohort showed a commitment to racial equality; they were also the ones most likely to continue as teachers.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-130)
When the Republicans came to power in the Southern states after 1867, they created the first system of taxpayer-funded public schools. Southern Blacks wanted public schools for their children but they did not demand racially integrated schools. Almost all the new public schools were segregated, apart from a few in New Orleans. After the Republicans lost power in the mid-1870s, conservative whites retained the public school systems but sharply cut their funding. [[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-131)
Howard University was founded in 1867, making it one of a number of historically black colleges and universities established after the American Civil War

#### Schools for Black students
Almost all private academies and colleges in the South were strictly segregated by race.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-132) The American Missionary Association supported the development and establishment of several historically black colleges, such as Fisk University and Shaw University. In this period, a handful of northern colleges accepted black students. The Oneida Institute of Science and Industry (founded 1827) was the first institution of higher education to routinely admit African-American men and provide mixed-race college-level education.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-133) Oberlin College (founded 1833) was the first mainly white, degree-granting college to admit African-American students.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-134) However, before the Civil War it is likely that only 3–5% of Oberlin students were African-American.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-135) By 1900, 400 African-Americans had earned B.A. degrees from Harvard, Yale, Oberlin, and 70 other "leading colleges."[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-136) Northern denominations and their missionary associations especially established private schools across the South to provide secondary education. They provided a small amount of collegiate work. Tuition was minimal, so churches supported the colleges financially, and also subsidized the pay of some teachers. In 1900, churches—mostly based in the North—operated 247 schools for blacks across the South, with a budget of about $1 million.

#### Growth of human capital
American post-elementary schooling was designed to be consistent with national needs. It stressed general and widely applicable skills not tied to particular occupations or geographic areas, in order that students would have flexible employment options. As the economy was dynamic, the emphasis was on portable skills that could be used in a variety of occupations, industries, and regions.[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-205)

### Colleges in 19th century
#### Schools for Black students
[edit]
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Freedmen's_school,_Edisto_Island,_S.C.)_-_Samuel_A._Cooley,_photographer,_Savannah,_Ga.,_Hilton_Head,_S.C.,_Beaufort,_S.C_LCCN2010647918_(cropped).jpg)
The Freedmen's School of Edisto Island, South Carolina photographed c.1865
In the early days of the Reconstruction era, the [Freedmen's Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedmen's_Bureau "Freedmen's Bureau") opened 1000 schools across the South for black children. This was essentially building on schools that had been established in numerous large contraband camps. Freedmen were eager for schooling for both adults and children, and the enrollments were high and enthusiastic. Overall, the Bureau spent $5 million to set up schools for blacks. By the end of 1865, more than 90,000 freedmen were enrolled as students in these schools. The school curriculum resembled that of schools in the North.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-127)

### Colleges in 19th century
#### Schools for Black students
Many Bureau teachers were well-educated Yankee women motivated by religion and abolitionism. W.E.B. DuBois wrote of the zealous spirit and success of what he referred to as "the crusade of the New England schoolma'am."[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-128) Half the teachers were southern whites; one-third were blacks, and one-sixth were northern whites.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-129) Most were women but among African Americans, male teachers slightly outnumbered female teachers. In the South, people were attracted to teaching because of the good salaries, at a time when the societies were disrupted and the economy was poor. Northern teachers were typically funded by northern organizations and were motivated by humanitarian goals to help the freedmen. As a group, only the black cohort showed a commitment to racial equality; they were also the ones most likely to continue as teachers.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-130)
When the Republicans came to power in the Southern states after 1867, they created the first system of taxpayer-funded public schools. Southern Blacks wanted public schools for their children but they did not demand racially integrated schools. Almost all the new public schools were segregated, apart from a few in New Orleans. After the Republicans lost power in the mid-1870s, conservative whites retained the public school systems but sharply cut their funding. [[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-131)
Howard University was founded in 1867, making it one of a number of historically black colleges and universities established after the American Civil War

### Colleges in 19th century
#### Schools for Black students
Almost all private academies and colleges in the South were strictly segregated by race.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-132) The American Missionary Association supported the development and establishment of several historically black colleges, such as Fisk University and Shaw University. In this period, a handful of northern colleges accepted black students. The Oneida Institute of Science and Industry (founded 1827) was the first institution of higher education to routinely admit African-American men and provide mixed-race college-level education.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-133) Oberlin College (founded 1833) was the first mainly white, degree-granting college to admit African-American students.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-134) However, before the Civil War it is likely that only 3–5% of Oberlin students were African-American.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-135) By 1900, 400 African-Americans had earned B.A. degrees from Harvard, Yale, Oberlin, and 70 other "leading colleges."[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-136) Northern denominations and their missionary associations especially established private schools across the South to provide secondary education. They provided a small amount of collegiate work. Tuition was minimal, so churches supported the colleges financially, and also subsidized the pay of some teachers. In 1900, churches—mostly based in the North—operated 247 schools for blacks across the South, with a budget of about $1 million.

### Colleges in 19th century
#### Schools for Black students
They employed 1600 teachers and taught 46,000 students.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-137)[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-138) Prominent schools included Howard University, a federal institution based in Washington; Fisk University in Nashville, Atlanta University, Hampton Institute in Virginia, and many others. Most new colleges in the 19th century were founded in northern states.
In 1890, Congress expanded the land-grant program to include federal support for state-sponsored colleges across the South. It required states to identify colleges for black students as well as white ones in order to get land grant support. This second Morrill Land-Grant Act thus simultaneously provided increased higher educational opportunities for African Americans but encouraged segregation.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-139)

### Colleges in 19th century
#### Schools for Black students
Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute was of national importance because it set the standards for what was called industrial education.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnderson198833%E2%80%9378-140)Booker T. Washington, one of its graduates, founded the influential Tuskegee Normal School for Colored Teachers in 1881. Washington championed industrial education for African Americans on the basis of its practicality, whereas W.E.B. DuBois emphasized the importance of offering African Americans the opportunity to prove themselves equal to whites by succeeding in traditional, classically-oriented B.A. degree programs.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-141) In 1900 relatively few black students were enrolled in college-level work because their schools were understaffed and underfunded and the students needed remedial study. The alumni of Keithley became high school teachers.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-142) However, some HBCUs—such as Howard University, Fisk University, and Atlanta University—had standard B.A. programs with classical curricula.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-143)
While the colleges and academies were generally coeducational, until the late 20th century, historians had taken little notice of the role of women as students and teachers.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-144)

### Consolidation: the passing of the one room schoolhouse
#### Growth of human capital
American post-elementary schooling was designed to be consistent with national needs. It stressed general and widely applicable skills not tied to particular occupations or geographic areas, in order that students would have flexible employment options. As the economy was dynamic, the emphasis was on portable skills that could be used in a variety of occupations, industries, and regions.[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-205)
Public schools were funded and supervised by independent districts that depended on taxpayer support. In dramatic contrast to the centralized systems in Europe, where national agencies made the major decisions, the American districts designed their own rules and curricula.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-206)

### Consolidation: the passing of the one room schoolhouse
#### Teachers and administrators
[edit]
Early public school superintendents emphasized discipline and rote learning, and school principals made sure the mandate was imposed on teachers. Disruptive students were expelled.[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-207)
Support for the high school movement occurred at the grass-roots level of local cities and school systems. After 1916, the federal government began to provide for vocational education funding as part of support for raising readiness to work in industrial and artisan jobs. In these years, states and religious bodies generally funded teacher training colleges, often called "normal schools". Gradually they developed full four-year curriculums and developed as state colleges after 1945.
Teachers organized themselves during the 1920s and 1930s. In 1917, the National Education Association (NEA) was reorganized to better mobilize and represent teachers and educational staff. The rate of increase in membership was constant under the chairmanship of James Crabtree—from 8,466 members in 1917 to 220,149 in 1931. The rival American Federation of Teachers (AFT) was based in large cities and formed alliances with the local labor unions. The NEA identified as an upper-middle-class professional organization, while the AFT identified with the working class and the union movement.[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-208)[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-209)

### Consolidation: the passing of the one room schoolhouse
#### Teachers and administrators
When liberals regained control of Congress in 1964, they passed numerous Great Society programs supported by President Lyndon B. Johnson to expand federal support for education. The Higher Education Act of 1965 set up federal scholarships and low-interest loans for college students, and subsidized better academic libraries, ten to twenty new graduate centers, several new technical institutes, classrooms for several hundred thousand students, and twenty-five to thirty new community colleges a year. A separate education bill enacted that same year provided similar assistance to dental and medical schools. On an even larger scale, the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965 began pumping federal money into local school districts.[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-210)

### Segregation and integration
[edit]
Segregation laws in the United States prior to _Brown v. Board of Education_
For much of its history, education in the United States was segregated (or even only available) based upon race. Early integrated schools such as the Noyes Academy, founded in 1835, in Canaan, New Hampshire, often were met with fierce local opposition. For the most part, African Americans received very little to no formal education before the Civil War. Some free blacks in the North managed to become literate. In cities, such a Philadelphia and New York City, they founded literary societies for self-education, as well as some academies for their children. The most prominent of the latter was Philadelphia's Institute for Colored Youth, the nation's first coeducational high school for African Americans.[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-211) A few institutions of higher education also were available to African Americans in the North. The Oneida Institute of Science and Industry was the first such entity to recruit and commonly admit African American men. New York Central College also was mixed race, and Oberlin College was the first B.A. degree-granting, white college to accept African Americans. In 1840, Oberlin bestowed the first known B.A. degree on an African American--George B. Vashon, who later was a founding member of the Howard University faculty.[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-212)

### Segregation and integration
In the South where slavery was legal, many states had laws prohibiting teaching enslaved African Americans to read or write.[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-213) A few taught themselves, sometimes in secret schools,[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-214) others learned from white playmates or more generous masters, but most were not able to learn to read and write. Schools for free people of color were privately run and supported, as were most of the limited schools for white children. Poor white children did not attend school. The wealthier planters hired tutors for their children and sent them to private academies and colleges at the appropriate age.
During Reconstruction a coalition of freedmen and white Republicans in Southern state legislatures passed laws establishing public education. The [Freedmen's Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedmen's_Bureau "Freedmen's Bureau") was created as an agency of the military governments that managed Reconstruction. It set up schools in many areas and tried to help educate and protect freedmen during the transition after the war. With the notable exception of the desegregated public schools in New Orleans, the schools were segregated by race. By 1900 more than 30,000 black teachers had been trained and put to work in the South, and the literacy rate had climbed to more than 50%, a major achievement in little more than a generation.[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_the_United_States#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnderson1988244%E2%80%93245-215)
Many colleges were set up for blacks; some were state schools like Booker T. Washington's Tuskegee Institute in Alabama, others were private ones subsidized by Northern missionary societies.
